title: W.Va. Supreme Court hears State BOE v. Sec. of State arguments - WSAZ
content: CHARLESTON, W.Va. (WSAZ) - Lawyers for the West Virginia Board of Education and for Secretary of State Kris Warner made arguments Tuesday in front of the state Supreme Court over the authority of the state Legislature to review and reject state Board of Education rule-making. The arguments go back to HB 2755, with lawyers for the West Virginia Board of Education, arguing that it violates the West Virginia Constitution, and closely resembles a 1988 ruling that was in favor of the state school board. Attorneys for the Secretary of State’s office say the bill’s language is nuanced enough to create different questions, and to cover the court’s concerns from the 38-year old ruling.

title: Czechia v Great Britain: how the tie was won - Billie Jean King Cup
content: The 2026 Billie Jean King Cup by Gainbridge Finals roared into life at the Shenzhen Bay Sports Centre as the World Cup of Tennis continues to deliver pulsating action, compelling storylines and a bucket load of national pride. Last week it was the turn of Davis Cup by Generali, now is the time for Billie Jean King Cup – the largest annual women’s international team competition in sport – to shine. For the remainder of this week, Billie Jean King Cup is the hottest ticket in town as eight nations, all of whom have earned the right to contest the Finals, battle to be crowned champions. The famous Billie Blue jackets also await the winners. The first nations to put their heads above the parapet were 11-time champions Czechia and Great Britain, who have been making moves in recent years and displaying unity as well as the ability to shock and surprise. After their impressive victory over Australia in Melbourne during April’s Qualifiers – a victory which propelled them to this stage of the competition – captain Anne Keothavong set out Great Britain’s stall in no uncertain terms. “Winning this competition is always the ultimate goal – I know we have got the players and the strength in depth in Great Britain to do something special in this competition,” she said. That was a statement of intent and for periods of this tie in looked as though Great Britain could reach the Billie Jean King Cup semi-finals for the third consecutive year and for the fourth time in five years. Ultimately, however, Czechia proved too strong – but not by much. That said, Marie Bouzkova and Linda Noskova did dispatch Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter respectively to fire their nation into an unassailable 2-0 lead. Next stop for Czechia, the semi-finals. While the opening singles match does not determine a tie's outcome, it is crucial and Bouzkova had just enough to defeat Kartal 7-6(2) 4-6 6-4 and set Czechia on their way. Huge credit goes to both players. Bouzkova held her nerve in what was a tense, physical clash and one which lasted one minute shy of three hours. Bouzkova is no stranger to a marathon match, but she is delivering when her nation needs it the most. After all, the 28-year-old won the decisive fifth match – Qualifier ties are best-of-five matches – against Viktorija Golubic as Czechia overcame Switzerland in Biel during April’s Qualifiers to seal their place at these Finals. While defeat naturally hurts, Kartal should take pride from her performance with this her competitive comeback following six months on the sidelines after suffering a stress fracture to her lower back at Indian Wells in March. Kartal had opportunities and, after winning the second set to level the match, she landed an early blow in the third to put herself in the driving seat. From that moment, however, her challenge faltered and Bouzkova came storming back. “She [Kartal] played incredibly,” said Bouzkova. “Not playing for half a year and coming out the way she did, huge respect for her. The last time she played, she played really well. It seems like she kept the momentum going even with a half-year break.” Ultimately, winning is all that matters and world No. 26 Bouzkova found a way. She also played some lovely tennis, including three wonderous backhands to put herself 3-2 up in the third set. Bouzkova’s victory laid a very solid platform for the Czechs and, with Noskova – a Grand Slam champion no less – in their ranks, a quiet confidence about victory would not be outlandish. Noskova duly delivered in the tie's second singles match, overcoming world No. 54 Katie Boulter 6-2 7-6(3), but she did not have it all her own way. Indeed, Boulter, like Kartal, had her moments and looked far removed from a player who had won just two of her last nine matches. The first set was perhaps more one-sided than it might have been, but Boulter took her opponent all the way in the second, with Noskova needing a tiebreak to shake off her would-be victor. Noskova, who fired down 15 aces during the clash, seemed to unleash greater attacking intent during the tiebreak and powered herself to victory with little to no fuss at all. In short, a very satisfying first outing at the Finals for Czechia. It was a tense back-and-forth tussle between Bouzkova and Kartal and, understandably, the latter may have felt an element of fatigue during the latter stages. That said, Kartal was right in this match for long periods, only for a third-set momentum shift to snatch away any thoughts of victory. There were a few key moments, but Bouzkova breaking straight back to level at 2-2 in the third set was a moment of consequence. Despite a late Kartal rally, the Czech did not look back from there. Indeed, Bouzkova breaking straight back after being broken herself in that third set completely altered the trajectory of this tie. That moment preceded Bouzkova winning four straight games and surging to the brink of victory. The 28-year-old may have left the door slightly ajar for Kartal, but she delivered the knockout blow with a further break of serve. That was the key play because the opening singles match could have gone either way before Bouzkova conjured victory. That fired Czechia into a 1-0 lead in the tie ahead of the second singles match. At that stage, Czechia were one further match-win from victory and Bouzkova’s win laid the foundations for Noskova to settle matters. Had the opening singles match gone the other way, an element of jeopardy would have remained. It is worth considering just who Czechia have sat on their bench as captain. Barbora Strycova is now in the hotseat after taking over from the long-serving and hugely successful Petr Pala ahead of April’s Qualifiers. In terms of Strycova’s CV, the 40-year-old represented Czechia in Billie Jean King Cup between 2002 and 2018, and she is one of five players in the competition’s history to win six or more competition titles. She is also one of two Czech players to do so, with the other being Petra Kvitova. Both won titles with Czechia in 2011-12, 2014-16 and 2018. What an individual for the current crop of Czech talent to have in their corner. Noskova: “The vision is to win the title, otherwise we wouldn’t be here. Everybody wants to win it. It’s a very competitive tournament and there are a lot of great players in each country. It is never easy.” Bouzkova: “This is what this competition is about – making all decisions as a team and finding a way through as a team. “More than anything, I am so happy to be part of this team. They pushed me forward. It was a team effort, and I am super happy we pulled this one through all together. Everything is more special when the stakes are as high as they get.” Kartal: “These events are my favourite, but they also sting the most.” Strycova: “I enjoyed every minute of it. It’s a privilege to have such a team. Being a captain of these amazing girls, they are just big champions. I’m enjoying being captain, every minute of it.” Keothavong: “For both Sonay and Katie, it required their absolute best and a bit of luck for the result to go our way. I can’t fault their efforts. I think the Czechs are the strongest team here – I’d be surprised if they don’t go on to win this competition.” Victory propels Czechia into the Billie Jean King Cup semi-finals where they will face the winners of Wednesday’s quarter-final between Kazakhstan and Spain. Czechia will next be in action on Friday. MORE: Kazakhstan vs Spain preview | All you need to know about 2026 BJK Cup Finals This is the first time since 2023 that Czechia, who are making their fifth appearance at a Finals, have reached the semi-finals as they continue their quest for a first Billie Jean King Cup title since 2018. Their last title came during a period of domination in the women’s World Cup of Tennis when Czechia, under the captaincy of Pala, built a Billie Jean King Cup dynasty. Can they end their wait for silverware? Time will tell.

content: Fresh off the premiere of “Earle Meets World,” Ashtin talks beauty rituals, tips from her sisters, and life after the cameras stop rolling Fresh off the premiere of “Earle Meets World,” Ashtin talks beauty rituals, tips from her sisters, and life after the cameras stop rolling Long before she was the cover star of MACzine, Ashtin Earle wore Ruby Woo lipstick for Christmas dance performances. In conversation, she revisits that childhood memory in a new interview with the MAC, published just weeks after the premiere of “Earle Meets World.” The Netflix show starring her family. Since her childhood dance performances, Earle’s makeup routine has shifted toward darker, cool tones. She often pairs MAC’s Stone or Plum lip pencil with Lipglass, rarely wears pink on her lips, and sometimes skips mascara altogether have influenced her routine, too: one encouraged her to thin her brows, while her younger sister Izabelle is the person she trusts most to do her makeup. The conversation moves beyond makeup when Ashtin explains the joke behind her social media bio, “tall, dark, & handsome.” She wrote it in high school and left it there, though its boldness does not quite match how she feels in person. Despite sharing so much of her life online, she says she is shy and takes time to warm up to people. With “Earle Meets World” bringing her family to a wider audience, the MACzine cover puts Ashtin in focus. She speaks for herself about the makeup she loves, the advice she takes from her sisters, and the shyness that may surprise people who know her only from social media. title: Mopar Collector Shows Rare V-Code Cuda, Challenger T/A, High-Impact Road Runner, Plus a Camaro SS - autoevolution
content:
Fortunately, there are still people who don’t look beyond the metal, glass, vinyl, rubber, and hydrocarbons. Quite the contrary, they take all those at face value, and treat cars – proper classic muscle icons – like what they are. I’ll bet that, if they ever were to attend a posh auction where Washington’s whisky would be offered, and they’d buy it, they’d take out the cork and pour a shot, right there, at the table. Because that’s what it was distilled for - to be enjoyed tastefully (pun intended). One such true car guy who firmly rejects that museum mentality showcased his collection (collection, maybe) on Joshuan Thomas’ YouTube channel (DezzysSpeedShop). This collector keeps his incredible fleet of vintage American muscle right in a working garage, happily sharing space with lawnmowers, spare parts, and giant spiders. He prefers driving his mechanical ogres, putting real miles on the odometer, and proving that classic cars belong on the asphalt. The undisputed veteran of the garage is a black 1970 Dodge Challenger T/A, a car the owner has proudly possessed for 28 years. This is not a pampered trailer queen, but a battle-scarred road warrior that has been driven hard on long road trips, including a memorable journey to Idaho. It proudly wears a layer of authentic road grime, and the rear window features a set of cool aftermarket louvers. Under the hood of the Challenger, the owner made a very clever mechanical choice. Instead of risking the original, highly valuable engine, he pulled it out for safekeeping and built a powerful 340 cubic-inch stroker motor for daily driving duties. Paired with a robust transmission, this stroker engine turns the Challenger into an absolute monster on the street. He actually recently scratched the quarter panel while backing into a ladder. Knight in shining armor? Those have never had their steel tested in battle. While it is surrounded by Dodge and Plymouth muscle, the Camaro holds its own with a timeless body style and a highly desirable matching-numbers factory original powertrain pedigree. Despite its undeniable charm, the wife has decided to part ways with the Camaro, offering it for sale with a firm price tag of $35,000. It is a solid project for the right buyer, as the owner notes that absolutely everything is included to finish the car. The interior needs to be put back together completely, but possessing a matching-numbers Chevy makes it an incredibly tempting restoration proposition. The owner has held onto this rare machine for an astonishing 30 years, yet he has never actually driven it (even he has one of those garage art artifacts. For now). Seeing the freshly painted body finally bolted back together has clearly sparked a renewed sense of true automotive excitement. This purple 'Cuda is a remarkably well-optioned factory monster, boasting a highly coveted V-code 440 cubic-inch Six-Barrel V8 mated to a 4-speed manual transmission. It also features a rare painted top, rather than the typical vinyl roof, alongside a fantastic factory Shaker hood. Currently, the massive engine is at the assembly shop. Rounding out the visible Mopar muscle is a striking 1970 Plymouth Road Runner painted in an eye-searing Sublime color, complete with a menacing black stripe and the iconic Air Grabber hood. This bold B-body sits quietly in the back of the shop, but it is fully functional and ready to unleash mechanical fury. It perfectly embodies the unapologetic, loud, and proud ethos of the classic American muscle car era. The Road Runner is currently equipped with a Quick Fuel carburetor, and the owner is steadily dialing in the engine to achieve peak street performance. In true gearhead fashion, he drives it aggressively enough that a recent burnout literally twisted the exhaust system out of alignment. That is exactly how these glorious machines are meant to be treated, proving that burning fuel – and rubber – will always beat letting a prized classic go to waste in a bubble cover. After nearly two decades in news television, Răzvan turned to a different medium. He’s been a field journalist, a TV producer, and a seafarer but found that he feels right at home among petrolheads.

title: E/V Nautilus Explores Uncharted Seamounts in Papahānaumokuākea Sanctuary - environment coastal & offshore
content: On September 22, Ocean Exploration Trust and partners on Exploration Vessel (E/V) Nautilus set sail for a 20-day expedition to explore previously unsurveyed deep-sea habitats around the Hawaiian Islands and within Papahānaumokuākea National Marine Sanctuary. This final expedition of the 2026 season will utilize the remotely operated vehicle (ROV), seafloor mapping, and telepresence systems of E/V Nautilus to explore never-before-seen ridges and seamounts in the eastern portion of Papahānaumokuākea National Marine Sanctuary and abyssal plain habitats southwest of the Main Hawaiian Islands. This expedition is funded by NOAA Ocean Exploration via the NOAA Ocean Exploration Cooperative Institute. “Most of the far offshore waters around Hawaiʻi have never been surveyed with modern technologies, and we are excited to share our expedition findings in real time with audiences of all ages,” said Dr. Daniel Wagner, OET Chief Scientist. The onboard expedition team is composed of scientists, engineers, mariners, educators, and students with many decades of deep-sea research experience, and includes 10 local representatives from the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, University of Hawaiʻi at Hilo, Molokai High School, Pacific Blue Studios, Bernice P. Bishop Museum, and Papahānaumokuākea National Marine Sanctuary. The onboard expertise will be supplemented with scientists from around the world, who will support the expedition remotely thanks to the ship’s advanced telepresence technology. Throughout the expedition, live footage from ROV dives and seafloor mapping surveys will stream around the clock via NautilusLive.org, allowing anyone with an Internet connection to watch and join the excitement of exploration and discovery. “At over 582,000 square miles, Papahānaumokuākea National Marine Sanctuary is the largest marine protected area within the National Marine Sanctuary System,” said Eric Roberts, sanctuary superintendent. “Through the use of cutting-edge technologies, this expedition will collect data to fill critical gaps in ocean knowledge and support US and international scientific priorities, including our understanding of deep-sea habitats, especially abyssal plain habitats and unexplored ridges that have rarely been seen around Hawaiʻi.” While nearshore waters around the islands have been relatively well surveyed, many offshore areas remain completely unexplored, hindering efforts to manage this unique region effectively. The team will collect acoustic mapping data and then use ROVs to survey deep-sea habitats up to 6,000 meters (19,685 feet/3.7 miles/3,280 fathoms) below the waves, gathering high-resolution seafloor imagery and environmental data. In addition to using the standard equipment aboard E/V Nautilus, the expedition will deploy a new oceanographic tool: the recently developed Quokka eDNA sampler from the Australian National Science Agency, which filters surface seawater to autonomously collect environmental DNA for biodiversity studies as the ship is underway. “During this expedition, we will get a rare opportunity to survey Cretaceous volcanic and abyssal geological history preserved within Papahānaumokuākea, which will help us learn and share a more complete, richer tectonic history of Hawaiian waters,” said Co-Lead Scientist Dr. Val Finlayson, University of Maryland. “Every rock we bring aboard tells its own story, and a small part of a much bigger story of the Central Pacific. Having the privilege of being able to use OET’s technology to access these remote, unexplored, and in some cases deepest parts of Hawaiian waters will open up new research avenues and from there, new opportunities to explore and learn about our ocean.” ROV dives will gather data to characterize deep-ocean habitats, biodiversity, bathymetry, and geological formations. This data helps establish a scientific baseline that future research, resource management, and responsible ocean stewardship decisions depend on. All data from E/V Nautilus expeditions are publicly archived with no embargo or access restrictions to ensure that deep-sea data is permanently available. Mapping and ROV operations will directly contribute to the US National Strategy for Ocean Mapping, Exploration, and Characterization, the Seabed 2030 initiative, and the NOAA ‘Omics Strategy. As is always the case with OET expeditions, community outreach is a key part of this expedition’s goals. Viewers across the Pacific and around the world are invited to participate in exploration: audiences can engage with the team at sea, ask questions, and receive real-time behind-the-scenes updates via NautilusLive.org and social media. Classrooms or community events are invited to connect with the at-sea team of STEAM professionals via free educational Q&A interactions. This is OET’s sixth expedition conducted in 2026, the 19th expedition conducted in Hawaiian waters since 2018, and the 182nd mission conducted since E/V Nautilus‘ inaugural season in 2009. Throughout this time, OET’s mission has remained the same: to use cutting-edge technologies in order to explore our fascinating underwater world and to engage curious minds of all ages along the way. title: Lopez ordered to defend world title v Catterall - Yahoo Sports
content: Teofimo Lopez has been ordered to defend his WBA world title against Briton Jack Catterall. Lopez became the WBA 'super' welterweight champion with a points win over Rolando Romero last month. Catterall, 33, is Lopez's mandatory challenger but the American has been campaigning to fight WBC champion Ryan Garcia in a unification bout instead. The WBA has now announced they expect Lopez to fight Catterall next, and the two parties have until 22 October to reach an agreement or there will be a purse bid. Catterall became the number one challenger and WBA 'regular' title-holder after beating Shakhram Giyasov in May. He acknowledged the WBA's ruling on X, saying: "Hi Teofimo Lopez." The Chorley native last fought for a world title in 2022 when he was controversially beaten by then undisputed light-welterweight champion Josh Taylor. Lopez, a three-weight world champion, could withdraw from negotiations and relinquish his world title, which may lead to Catterall being upgraded to world champion. Lopez attended the Garcia v Conor Benn fight week in Las Vegas earlier this month and was stopped from entering the ring after Garcia's quick win. Catterall has just two defeats on his record - to Taylor and American Arnold Barboza Jr - with 33 wins and 14 stoppages. Lopez, 29, also has two losses during his career, a 2021 points loss to George Kambosos Jr and more recently a decision defeat by Shakur Stevenson in January. title: Next-gen GM V-8 Engines: More Displacement, More Power, More Torque - The ClassicCars.com Journal
content: Includes the most powerful naturally-aspirated V-8 in the segment Sometimes I wonder if the world would be a better place if every automotive manufacturer had a Tim “The Toolman” Taylor around to remind engineers, designers, and mechanics to add “MORE POWER!” to all new automobiles. To my knowledge, General Motors hasn’t hired Tim Taylor, but its new iteration of small-blocks would make him let out a celebratory grunt. “These new V-8 engines advance GM’s legendary Small Block architecture with greater capability, more advanced technology and the strength of GM’s manufacturing footprint behind them,” says Tom Bishop, chief engineer for Small Block engines. “They’re engineered to provide truck customers the confidence and performance they expect from a GM V-8.” Slated for the next generation of Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra models, the new 5.7- and 6.6-liter V-8s deliver more displacement, horsepower, and torque. Previously, the selection for light-duty pickups were a 5.3- or 6.2-liter V-8; enthusiasts may note that the new engines measure 350 and 400 cubic-inches, respectively. The improvements in horsepower and torque are due to four things, according to GM engineers: The new 5.7-liter V-8 will put out 402 horsepower and 428 lb-ft of torque. GM touts that the Silverado 1500 will have a “best-in-class maximum available tow rating of 13,700 pounds when properly equipped.” The larger 6.6-liter V-8 is rated at 481 horsepower and 501 lb-ft of torque. According to GM, it is the “most powerful naturally-aspirated V-8 engine in its class.” To see the full ratings, check out the chart below. Each gas engine will also include a dual-fuel system that combines direct injection and port fuel injection, along with a new lubrication system featuring a continuously variable oil pump, on-engine oil cooler, and reworked oil feed locations for greater oil pressure consistency. title: Lucid Seeks En Banc Review of Fifth Circuit Decision Upholding Texas Direct Sales Ban - The National Law Review

On September 4, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Texas officials and the Texas Automobile Dealers Association (TADA) in Lucid Group USA, Inc. v. Johnston in a decision following a line of Fifth Circuit cases dating back more than 20 years rejecting constitutional challenges to state bans on the direct sale by manufacturers of motor vehicles to consumers. The three-member panel unanimously found that circuit precedent compelled them to conclude Texas’s ban on manufacturer-owned dealerships, codified at Texas Occ. Code § 2301.476, withstood rational basis review under the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses. But in the decision, two of the justices—including the author of the lead opinion—concurred in the decision but questioned whether the Texas ban amounted to improper economic protectionism of in-state interests. On September 18, 2026, Lucid filed a petition seeking en banc review of the decision, opening the possibility the Fifth Circuit may soon revisit its prior decisions on this issue and consider whether state law direct sales bans violate protections afforded under the U.S. Constitution. Lucid Group, Inc. manufactures luxury electric vehicles, and its affiliate, Lucid Group USA, sells them online and through company owned retail locations called “studios.” Lucid has no franchised dealers in Texas or elsewhere. Texas Occupations Code § 2301.476 prohibits a motor vehicle manufacturer, as well as an affiliate or entity under common control, from directly or indirectly owning, operating, or controlling a dealership that sells the same type of vehicle. In 2021, the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles told Lucid that it could not sell vehicles at its Plano studio. Lucid sued the DMV officials in November 2022 under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, bringing as-applied challenges under the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the U.S. Constitution. TADA intervened. The district court denied the state defendants’ motion to dismiss in June 2023, but on March 31, 2025, granted summary judgment to the state defendants and Lucid appealed. The controlling issue was whether Texas’s direct sales ban, as applied to Lucid, violated the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses even though Lucid had no franchised dealers. Lucid argued that the law created an irrational distinction between direct sales manufacturers and both franchised manufacturers and independent dealers. Because the law involved neither a suspect class nor a fundamental right, the Court applied rational basis review, requiring Lucid to rule out every conceivable rational basis for the classification. A three-member panel of the Fifth Circuit affirmed, holding that Ford Motor Co. v. Texas Department of Transportation, 264 F.3d 493 (5th Cir. 2001), International Truck & Engine Corp. v. Bray, 372 F.3d 717 (5th Cir. 2004), and Tesla, Inc. v. Louisiana Automobile Dealers Ass’n, 113 F.4th 511 (5th Cir. 2024), controlled. The Court rejected Lucid’s proposed comparisons. Following Ford and Tesla, the Court treated the relevant class as all vehicle manufacturers, not only those using the franchise model. It held that Lucid was not similarly situated to independent dealers because § 2301.476 defines “manufacturer” to include affiliates and entities under common control, and Lucid’s manufacturing and retail entities fall within that definition. Even if the law treated different groups differently, the Court held that Texas could rationally limit vertical integration, monopolistic tendencies, and potential abuses in the automobile retail market. Citing Tesla, the Court described a manufacturer’s move into distribution as a classic example of vertical integration. Because Tesla and Lucid make the same product and use the same direct sales model, and because the Louisiana and Texas bans are similar, the Court held that Tesla foreclosed Lucid’s as-applied Equal Protection challenge as a matter of law. The Court rejected the substantive Due Process claim for the same reasons, explaining that rational basis review works the same way under both clauses. Both circuit judges who joined the panel opinion wrote separately to express reservations. Judge Higginbotham, who also wrote the panel opinion, questioned applying Tesla to Lucid. He traced direct sales bans to historical concerns about manufacturers exploiting franchised dealers through forced inventory purchases and at-will terminations, explaining that those concerns do not fit a manufacturer with no same-brand dealers to harm. He noted that vertical integration could lower consumer prices by avoiding double marginalization that results from using franchised dealers, and observed that limiting EV distribution could slow innovation and reduce consumer choice. Chief Judge Elrod also questioned whether Tesla foreclosed Lucid’s as-applied challenge under a different state’s law and whether the vertical integration rationale could be reconciled with Fifth Circuit decisions such as St. Joseph Abbey v. Castille, 712 F.3d 215 (5th Cir. 2013), which held that pure economic protectionism is not, on its face, a legitimate state interest. Both judges nevertheless agreed that existing Fifth Circuit precedent mandated the result. Perhaps emboldened by the doubts expressed by two of the three members of the panel, Lucid on September 18, 2026 filed a petition seeking en banc review of the decision. Under Rule 40(b)(2) of the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure, a party may seek en banc review only in limited circumstances, including when a panel decision conflicts with a decision of the court or where the proceeding “involves one or more questions of exceptional importance.” If a majority of the active circuit judges choose to grant this petition, Lucid may soon have the opportunity to argue why the Fifth Circuit should reconsider its prior decisions and determine whether Lucid should have an opportunity to present evidence that Texas’s law banning manufacturer-direct sales violates protections afforded under the U.S. Constitution. An intriguing international fixture with plenty of Liverpool-related interest takes place in Amsterdam on Thursday night. There, a Netherlands squad captained by Virgil van Dijk and also including Jeremie Frimpong, Cody Gakpo and Ryan Gravenberch will meet Germany, who will be, for the first time, managed by former Reds boss Jürgen Klopp. The UEFA Nations League tie at Johan Cruyff Arena will not feature Florian Wirtz, however. New head coach Klopp has selected 44 players for Die Mannschaft’s four upcoming games, with Wirtz among a group of 20 that will join up only for the matches against Serbia and Greece in early October. Further Liverpool connections can be found within the Germany set-up, though, with Peter Krawietz and Pepijn Lijnders reprising their roles as Klopp’s assistant coaches. Klopp signed Gakpo, Gravenberch and Van Dijk during his glorious reign at Anfield. The latter was a cornerstone of his all-conquering Reds team, while Gakpo and Gravenberch would also play key roles in the 2024-25 Premier League title-winning campaign under Arne Slot. Van Dijk sits just four appearances shy of reaching 100 caps for his country and he is set to achieve that milestone under another big-name debutant on the international management scene: Xavi Hernandez. The skipper recently held talks with the new Netherlands boss regarding his international future. And, following Liverpool’s win at AFC Bournemouth on Sunday, he explained that he realised quickly that he wished to continue leading Oranje under the legendary ex-Spain and Barcelona midfielder. “Obviously it was a massive decision,” Van Dijk said. “I had to feel the confidence and the combination of respect and joy and everything I wanted. “That was from the first second the case, so the conversation didn’t need to be that long. But it was very good, so I am really looking forward to meeting up tomorrow for the important four games. “Let's make the next two years at least an amazing time.” Xavi, meanwhile, echoed those comments during a press conference on Monday. He stated: “It was a really good meeting [with Van Dijk]. He was very honest, he has the capacity to continue. He’s a good leader, he’s positive, he’s motivated. title: Flyby v. Harvard Shuttle: A Petition for One Loop - thecrimson.com
content: Picture this. It’s 1 a.m. in the wee hours of the morning, and you are stumbling out of the Currier ten man. Bleary-eyed, you squint at PassioGo (rip) and try to figure out how the heck you are supposed to get back to Mather. Joke’s on you: only the overnight loop is running, and the next one isn’t coming for 30 minutes, and it won’t even get you back to the concrete towers. You decide the best course of action is just to splurge on the $12 Uber. It’s 8 a.m., and you are just finishing up your sports practice in the stadium, and you hop on the shuttle, destined to go back to Pfoho, only to realize that you got on the Allston Loop and you, in fact, will not be brought back to the Quad. You didn’t even know there were shuttles that didn’t go to the Quad. What’s the point of the shuttle then? It’s 2:25 p.m., and you have a class in Boylston at 2:45. However, it’s the middle of January and the snow is coming at you sideways, and all you want is to take the shuttle your university so graciously supplies. You figure 25 minutes is plenty of time, so you wait for the shuttle, as Citymapper says it will be here in just two minutes. Well, two minutes turns into 20, and now you are sliding through black ice just trying to get to the seminar your advisor said you had to be in. I say no more. As a junior in Cabot House, I am well acquainted with the Harvard shuttle system. Recently, I’ve been asked my opinion on the new shuttle app, Citymapper, versus its predecessor, PassioGo. The truth is that the app is not the issue. No amount of new features, shaky reliability, or different graphics can fix the fundamental issues that plague the Harvard Shuttle system. Currently, there are nine different shuttle routes. Nine. Why? I have no clue. We have an undergraduate campus so small that I can get from one end to the other (Quad to SEC) in eight minutes by bike, 15 minutes running, and 25 minutes walking. There is absolutely no reason that one shuttle cannot circumnavigate campus in 30 minutes or 40 max, factoring in stoppage time. Thus, I propose a new system: a loop to end all loops. Through meticulous Google Maps planning and contemplative thoughts on my Quad walk, I have devised an eight-stop shuttle system that allows for full campus coverage. Those eight stops include: The Quad, Cambridge Commons South, Kirkland, the Stadium, the SEC, Mather, the Inn, and Cambridge Commons North. How would this help? You ask. Well, I’ve thought about this, too. Instead of nine loops with stops that even a quadling couldn’t articulate, we’d have one shuttle loop. We put all of the shuttle buses on this one loop. Hypothetically, you would only need six shuttles on the loop at any given time to have a shuttle come every five minutes at any given stop, eight for a five-minute guarantee. Picture this. You go to any of the known shuttle stops (no more wondering how to get back to the Quad from the Yard), and a shuttle will come EVERY FIVE MINUTES. I know people who ask to leave class early just to catch a shuttle that won’t return for another twenty. Desperate times call for desperate measures. If Harvard cares about attendance, this is the solution. No more excuses for being late to class, no more asking to leave early. Once you get on that shuttle, you would know exactly where it was going and exactly where to get off. You would know the route like the back of your hand. Students wouldn’t need PassioGo or Citymapper or whatever the new iteration we’ll have next semester. The route is simple, reliable. You could travel from one end of the campus (Quad -> Stadium, SEC -> Cambridge Commons North) in 15 minutes flat. No longer is the Quad a sentence of exile on Housing Day. Just a simple, easy, ten-minute shuttle away. And I am a selfless petitioner. Do I, as a quadling, think that the shuttle needs to stop at Mather/the Inn/Kirkland? No. But I understand that we are proposing a dramatic change and some river Houses may need to be eased into it. They still covet a ride across the river that could be a ten-minute walk, and that’s okay. But what if you’re at Mather and need to get to the SEC? Or at Lamont and want a ride home to Kirkland? I have a simple solution. Walk to another shuttle stop, or walk to your destination. Currently, the stop outside Lamont doesn’t even take you to the Quad. You are the ones always bragging about how much more convenient being in the river is than being in the Quad. Let’s level the playing field and adopt the one-route policy. Time to test that theory out, folks. I am willing to flesh out the nitty-gritty details of stops and exact routes down to Cambridge’s many one-way streets. All I want, as a distant resident of Cabot House, is a system that finally works for me, instead of making me late to class. We hold so many gripes towards the university, from the new grade cap to the loss of HUDS takeout containers. So why not fix a problem that would likely save the university money (one route = fewer buses) and win them accolades from the student body they continually manage to aggravate? To the deans: the ball is in your court.

Combined with an enhanced version of the previous generation i-FLEX face structure, the result is more efficient energy transfer at impact. ZXi RKT woods were also engineered for greater consistency, using a new “Variable Roll Design” that helps keep misses on line. By optimizing performance across the face, a “Rebound Frame” technology boosts ball speed and distance by utilizing two flex zones, instead of one. “Throughout testing, one of the most consistent themes we heard from players was the desire for more speed across a larger area of the face without giving up consistency,” Patrick Ripp, Srixon Tour Engineering Manager, said in a release. “RKT Face was developed to answer that challenge. By combining several technologies into a single performance system, we were able to create a face that not only produces exceptional ball speed but does so more consistently across a wider range of impact locations. While improvements to the face have been established, engineers also targeted the acoustic element in building a golf club. The new “Acousticore” chassis utilizes an AI-optimized internal rib structure and lightweight carbon fiber crown construction for a crisper and more controlled sound at impact. Srixon also relied heavily on its successful Tour setup and PGA Tour players during the extensive prototyping phase that lasted over two years. The R&D team refined face depth, crown height, address profiles, face angles, and lie angles to create a more confident look and improved performance over previous generations, thanks to the help from players such as Ryan Fox, who won The Open Championship this summer with ZXi RKT in the bag. The deeper faces and taller heads increase performance high on the face, while more compact shapes provide a cleaner, more player-preferred appearance at address. Another aesthetically impactful design change is a redesigned laser face milling pattern that players believe improves alignment at address and helps maintain more consistent spin in challenging conditions. “One of the biggest differences with this generation of woods was how closely we worked alongside our Tour staff throughout the entire process,” Ripp added. “Every round of testing led to new insights, and those insights directly influenced the decisions our engineering team made. The final product is a lineup that reflects what elite players are asking for while delivering benefits that every golfer can appreciate. New ZXi RKT fairway woods and hybrids feature the same RKT Face architecture, while also introducing Srixon’s most comprehensive adjustability system yet. For the first time, both adjustable sole weights and and ajustable hosel sleeves allow golfers to dial in launch conditions, swing weight and distance gapping. The new ZXi RKT woods lineup is available at PGA Tour Superstore. Scotty Cameron announced Tuesday a limited-edition line of Onset Center (OC) putters with the new Phantom OC Spec III putters. This time, the select putters pair an all-black finish with high-contrast sightlines in two models: Phantom 5 and 11R OC. Scotty Cameron OC putters combine low-torque performance along with feel and feedback to promote a more square-to-the-stroke-path. This is achieved through the “Onset Center” shaft position, set back from the putter head’s leading edge (Onset) and aligned with its center of gravity (Center) to minimize torque and simplify the putting stroke. While some putters are considered zero torque, Scotty Cameron’s OC design is considered low-torque, with a small amount of putter rotation still made through the stroke. Scotty Cameron Phantom OC Spec III mallets share the name with highly optimized Spec III performance builds in the automotive world, where all components and modifications operate harmoniously to produce ultimate performance. Both the Phantom 5 and 11R OC are equipped with a glare-free, durable PVD black finish as well as three high-contrast sightlines to help enhance the alignment aid and frame the golf ball at address. Each model leverages Scotty’s chain-link face milling for a responsive, soft feel at impact, and is equipped with a custom black mid-size Matador grip and a black steel shaft. New Scotty Cameron Phantom OC Spec III putters are available at PGA TOUR Superstore. The Phantom 5 is a wingback design with a compact profile. The Phantom 11R is a stable, high-MOI mallet with a tour-inspired rounded shape. The Phantom 11R OC Spec III is available as a left-handed option. title: Israel vs Republic of Ireland - how Uefa Nations League matches became so contentious - BBC
content: Israel have not played a fixture on home soil for three years, since the beginning of the Gaza war, and have used Hungary as a home base for 10 fixtures in that time An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage. That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians. But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza. And on 4 October, the Republic of Ireland will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia. No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis. So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football? As soon as the Republic of Ireland were placed with Israel - plus Austria and Kosovo - at the Nations League draw in February, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) faced calls from some to boycott the matches because of Israel's military action in Gaza. In May a friendly match the Republic of Ireland played against Qatar in Dublin was twice interrupted after fans threw tennis balls onto the pitch featuring the Palestinian flag. The FAI eventually took a vote of its delegates in July, in which 75 members voted to play the matches and 32 voted to boycott. Not playing the matches could have harmed Irish football in the long-run, the FAI said, amid the possibility of Uefa sanctions for refusing to fulfil the fixtures and the potential loss of millions of euros in income. As well as curtailing its coverage, RTE will not take advertising or sponsorship income from the matches, saying it will only "meet its contractual obligations" to broadcast the fixtures. No tickets are being sold to Irish fans for either the 'home' or 'away' matches, with a small allocation available for Israeli fans for the first fixture, which has been the case at multiple previous Israel home games held in Hungary. How Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly. The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil". Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin. The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest. In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years. The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition. Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean. FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide". "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel." In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity". The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations". Fans of Irish Premier Division club Bohemians are among those who have protested against Ireland playing against Israel The Republic of Ireland has been among the European countries to most keenly show support for Palestinians since the start of Israel's military offensive in Gaza in October 2023. More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN). In May 2024, alongside Spain and Norway, Ireland officially recognised a Palestinian state, and later that year joined South Africa's Gaza genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice. The country has also boycotted Eurovision since 2025 because of Israel's ongoing participation in the song contest, was the first EU country to ban goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and has issued travel bans for Israeli government ministers. On Monday, Irish foreign minister Helen McEntee said: "Ireland's view is clear - international law is being breached. We are seeing an attempt to erase a population." Israel has criticised Ireland's standpoint and claims its actions in Gaza constitute self-defence, after the armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. The stands at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen, Hungary - where Israel have played six home fixtures in the past three years - will be empty for the match against the Republic of Ireland Last summer a UN commission of inquiry found that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, and this year a further investigation determined that the country has deliberately targeted children with military force, resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations it has committed genocide. The Republic of Ireland is not the only nation to have expressed reluctance to face Israel in international football. In 2024, Belgium refused to host Israel on home soil, and the match was held instead in Debrecen. The president of the Norwegian Football Association, Lise Klaveness, made a public statement last year saying Israel should be suspended from European competitions, and Turkey also called for Israel to be banned. In a statement released on Tuesday, Amnesty International said Uefa was "giving Israel an international stage" rather than "sending a clear message there is a cost" for its actions in Gaza. BBC Sport reported last autumn that Uefa executives were considering a vote on whether to ban Israel, under pressure from representatives from a number of nations. But any plan to hold a vote was pulled when the first phase of a ceasefire was announced last October. title: T-Mobile v DAIFI: Patent Settlements Need Objective Triggers for Post-PTP Payments - The National Law Review
content: The National Law Review uses cookies to track usage trends and patterns to better understand and improve our website. By using this website and/or clicking on any link on the website, you confirm your consent to the NLR’s placing and usage of cookies. Patent settlements are supposed to convert litigation uncertainty into contractual certainty. The precedential Federal Circuit decision of T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC, issued August 28, 2026, illustrates what can happen when a settlement resolves the infringement case but leaves the economic consequences of a pending Patent Office proceeding insufficiently defined. The dispute arose from a settlement and patent license that required T-Mobile to make an additional payment if an asserted patent claim “survives” an ex parte reexamination. Several claims were later confirmed as patentable without amendment, yet the parties disagreed about whether they had actually “survived” within the meaning of their agreement. That disagreement produced new litigation and, ultimately, a Federal Circuit decision holding that the case did not arise under patent law at all. The jurisdictional holding is important, but the broader transactional lesson may be more useful. When the economics of a patent settlement depend on future Patent Office action, the agreement should translate possible agency outcomes into specific contractual consequences. Familiar patent terminology is not a substitute for defining the bargain. KAIFI sued T-Mobile in the Eastern District of Texas for infringement of U.S. Patent No. 6,922,728, which concerned Wi-Fi calling technology. While the infringement litigation was pending, T-Mobile requested ex parte reexamination of the patent. Before the Patent Office completed that proceeding, the parties settled. Their January 2022 Settlement and Patent License Agreement provided T-Mobile with a license, required an initial payment, and established a second contingent payment, called the “EPR Payment,” if any identified “Asserted Claim survives the EPR.” The agreement also generally prohibited T-Mobile from challenging validity or enforceability, while carving out the reexamination that T-Mobile had already initiated. The Patent Office eventually confirmed seven of the eight asserted claims without amendment and found the eighth patentable as amended. T-Mobile nevertheless refused to make the additional payment. Its position was not simply that the Patent Office had canceled the claims. Instead, T-Mobile argued that KAIFI had taken positions during reexamination that materially altered claim scope from the positions it had advanced in the infringement litigation. T-Mobile also alleged inequitable conduct based on KAIFI’s handling of allegedly inconsistent claim-construction positions. The district court rejected that approach. It interpreted “survives” by reference to the formal outcome of the reexamination and concluded that claims confirmed as patentable without amendment had survived. It therefore entered summary judgment for KAIFI. The resulting appeal presented an unusual jurisdictional problem because both sides maintained that the Federal Circuit should hear the case. The Federal Circuit disagreed. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1), the Federal Circuit has exclusive appellate jurisdiction over specified district court cases arising under federal patent law. Under Christianson v. Colt Industries Operating Corp. and the Supreme Court’s federal-question framework in Gunn v. Minton, that category includes claims created by patent law and a limited class of state-law claims that necessarily raise a disputed and substantial federal issue. Because T-Mobile had initiated the case through a declaratory-judgment complaint, the court applied the approach reflected in ABB Inc. v. Cooper Industries, LLC: it considered the claim the declaratory defendant would have brought in a hypothetical well-pleaded complaint. Here, that claim was essentially KAIFI’s actual counterclaim for breach of contract under Texas law. That reframing proved decisive. The question was not whether patent doctrines appeared somewhere in T-Mobile’s arguments. They plainly did. The question was whether KAIFI had to establish a proposition of patent law in order to recover the contingent payment. The Federal Circuit concluded that it did not. Under 35 U.S.C. § 307(a), an ex parte reexamination concludes through formal Patent Office action canceling claims determined to be unpatentable, confirming patentable claims, and incorporating patentable amended or new claims. Seven asserted claims here had been confirmed without amendment. A court could therefore interpret the contract and the Reexamination Certificate and conclude that a claim had “survived” without deciding prosecution disclaimer or inequitable conduct. That alternative path was enough to defeat the requirement under Gunn that a federal issue be necessarily raised. The contrast with Jang v. Boston Scientific Corp. helps define the jurisdictional boundary. In Jang, a contract required additional compensation for sales of products covered by specified patents. Determining whether payment was due therefore required deciding whether the products infringed the patent claims. Patent infringement was not merely a defense or one possible interpretation of the dispute. It was embedded in the contractual liability determination itself. T-Mobile involved a different type of performance trigger. The agreement referred to whether an asserted claim “survives” a Patent Office proceeding. Because that language could plausibly be applied to the agency’s formal disposition of the claims, patent infringement, prosecution disclaimer, and inequitable conduct were not indispensable elements of the contract claim. The Federal Circuit transferred the appeal to the Fifth Circuit. The comparison matters beyond appellate procedure. Contract provisions can assign commercial significance to patent-law determinations in very different ways. A royalty tied expressly to whether a product practices or infringes a patent may require a court to decide substantive patent law. A payment tied to an objectively identified administrative event may instead present an ordinary question of contract interpretation. KAIFI separately argued that “survives” had become a patent-law term of art because courts routinely refer to patent claims as surviving reexamination or inter partes review. The Federal Circuit rejected that contention, concluding that those decisions used the word in its ordinary sense rather than as a specialized statutory or regulatory term. That conclusion carries a useful drafting lesson. Terminology can be common among patent lawyers without having a sufficiently precise legal meaning to allocate millions of dollars of contractual risk. The problem was particularly visible here because the parties had anticipated at least one source of uncertainty. During negotiations, they disagreed about whether an amended claim would count as having survived reexamination. Instead of resolving that issue, they memorialized the disagreement in a footnote. The dispute ultimately centered elsewhere because several claims were confirmed without amendment, but the drafting history exposes the larger problem: recognizing a contingency is not the same as allocating it. For settlements involving IPR, reexamination, post-grant review, or similar proceedings, the parties can often define the consequences directly. The agreement can distinguish claims confirmed without amendment, amended or substitute claims, canceled claims, and newly issued claims. It can address whether statements made during Patent Office proceedings that affect claim scope have contractual consequences. It can also specify when an agency determination becomes operative, including whether rehearing or appellate review must be exhausted. The same coordination is important for no-challenge provisions. T-Mobile sought to rely on alleged inequitable conduct even though the settlement contained a covenant restricting challenges to validity and enforceability. The Federal Circuit did not resolve the ultimate effect of that tension, but it illustrates why reservations concerning Patent Office conduct, enforceability, validity, or claim scope should be reconciled expressly with any no-challenge covenant. The Federal Circuit did not decide whether T-Mobile ultimately owes the contingent payment. That merits question now belongs to the Fifth Circuit under Texas contract law. Nor did the court hold that patent-related contractual disputes categorically fall outside Federal Circuit jurisdiction. Its holding is narrower: patent questions do not create Federal Circuit jurisdiction merely because they are important to a party’s preferred theory of a contract dispute. They must be necessary to resolving the claim and sufficiently substantial to the federal system. For technology companies, licensors, licensees, and others resolving patent disputes, the decision points to a broader objective. A settlement should not merely identify the future event on which the economics depend. It should define what each reasonably foreseeable outcome means. Patent litigation inevitably contains uncertainty. A well-designed settlement should allocate that uncertainty rather than preserve it in shorthand and send the parties back to court to determine what they agreed to. title: Aspirus Rhinelander Clinic Introduces Advanced Inspire V Device for Sleep Apnea Patients - Aspirus Health
content:
RHINELANDER, Wis. – Aspirus Rhinelander Clinic is pleased to offer the newest generation of Inspire therapy, Inspire V, an innovative implantable treatment option for patients living with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The advanced technology provides an alternative for individuals who have not found success with or are unable to tolerate traditional CPAP therapy. Dr. Ryan Black, Otolaryngologist at Aspirus Rhinelander Clinic, is now offering this state-of-the-art treatment to qualifying patients seeking long-term relief from sleep apnea symptoms. “Sleep apnea can have a profound impact on a person’s overall health, energy levels, and quality of life,” said Dr. Black. “Many patients become frustrated when CPAP therapy doesn't fit comfortably into their daily routine. Inspire V gives us another proven option that addresses the condition in a different way, helping patients breathe more naturally during sleep and improve their long-term health.” Inspire therapy has been available for more than 10 years and has helped thousands of patients nationwide better manage obstructive sleep apnea. Recent changes in insurance coverage, including expanded approval by Medicare and many private insurers, have increased access to the therapy for eligible individuals. The newest generation, Inspire V, features several important enhancements:
•	Simplified design: Eliminates the need for a sensing lead in the intercostal muscles.
•	Advanced technology: Utilizes an accelerometer within the neurostimulator battery to detect breathing directly from the chest wall.
•	Streamlined procedure: Enables a faster, less invasive implantation process and improved patient experience. “Inspire V reflects the continued evolution of sleep apnea treatment,” Dr. Black added. “The updated design allows for a more efficient procedure while maintaining the effectiveness patients expect. It’s exciting to bring this next-generation technology to northern Wisconsin and offer another pathway to healthier sleep.” Inspire therapy is an implantable neurostimulation system that works similarly to a pacemaker but is designed to treat moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea. The device delivers gentle stimulation to the hypoglossal nerve, which controls tongue movement. This stimulation helps keep the airway open during sleep, reducing apnea events and improving sleep quality. The Inspire system is implanted beneath the skin through two small incisions, one in the neck and one in the chest. It consists of three components:
•	A stimulation cuff lead placed around the hypoglossal nerve
•	A generator that houses the sensing mechanism which detects respiratory effort
•	An external remote that patients use to manage their therapy Clinical studies have demonstrated a 90% overall patient satisfaction rate with Inspire therapy. Inspire therapy is approved for adults age 18 and older who meet specific criteria, including:
•	Moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea (AHI 15-100)

title: Japan v India: Visitors avoid shock defeat after controversial wide is overturned - BBC
content: Axar Patel bowled the final over for India which included the overturned wide India 32-4 (5 overs): Iyer 16 (12); Hara-Hinze 2-17 Japan 30-3 (5 overs): Kadowaki-Fleming 12 (12); Washington 2-13 World champions India avoided a shock defeat by Japan with a tense two-run win after a wide ball was controversially overturned in the final over. In the one-off T20, which was reduced to five overs a side, Japan needed eight off the final over after their bowlers had remarkably restricted cricketing juggernauts India to 32-4. Left-hander Alexander Shirai-Patmore was attempting to reverse-sweep spinner Axar Patel and the ball passed down what would have been the leg side if he had not changed his stance. The umpire signalled a wide. After the umpire's signal, Axar was visibly frustrated with the decision and disputed the call alongside captain Shreyas Iyer. The two umpires had a discussion after India's complaints and the decision was overturned, significantly taking the equation to six runs needed off three balls instead of five off four. Axar then closed out the over to finish with figures of 0-7 off two overs and Japan finished agonisingly short on 30-3. In white-ball cricket, any delivery bowled down the leg side is usually called a wide, but the ICC's playing conditions for men's T20 internationals state a batter loses those privileges from the moment he or she changes the position of their hands or feet to play a reversed shot. Essentially, if a reverse sweep is attempted, the guidelines say both sides of the wicket should be treated as the off side. This suggests the correct decision was reached eventually, but the incident has gained attention for how it was overturned despite there being no decision review system (DRS) in place for the match. The preamble for the playing conditions also refers to the "spirit of cricket", with "accept the umpire's decision" listed as one of these points, although this is not one of the game's laws. It was an agonising near-miss for Japan, who had struggled early on in their chase as they stuttered to 8-2 after two overs before taking 17 off the next two, which kept them in contention before the dramatic finale. With the ball, they were led by 17-year-old spinner Charlie Hara-Hinze who took 2-17, including the wicket of destructive opener Abhishek Sharma first ball, before Shreyas' 16 off 12 balls provided some relief from his side being 14-3. It was the first time the teams had played each other internationally because Japan have never reached a T20 World Cup, and the game was played in preparation for the men's Asian Games which start on 24 September. Earlier, India cruised to victory in the women's Asian Games final as they thrashed Sri Lanka by 147 runs. title: Storylines | RSL v. Seattle: Road Battle With Plenty at Stake - Real Salt Lake
content: Attention now turns to Lumen Field as Real Salt Lake hits the road for yet another midweek match, this time at Seattle against the Sounders. With Mastroeni’s men looking to snap a 12-game winless streak, the Claret-and-Cobalt must leave it all on the pitch as it heads into battle with hopes of earning its first MLS victory since May 16. In this edition of Storylines, we’ll take a closer look at RSL’s recent run of form, the key players who will be called upon to step up on Wednesday, those who will miss the match due to international duty, and the midweek opponent, Seattle Sounders FC. The Claret-and-Cobalt head into another road midweek matchup with something to prove. After falling to Vancouver 3-0 at home on Saturday, RSL suffered back-to-back home shutouts for the first time since April 2025. In order to avoid setting a new all-time single-season winless run of 13 straight matches, the visitors now look to its leaders and the key roster pieces that helped boost RSL near the top of the standings earlier in the season. Although Real Salt Lake has found itself in an unfavorable run of form with a record number of players out due to injury, suspension or visa issues, the squad still believes it has an arsenal of young weapons rostered and a few key players who can make a world of difference. With RSL star MF Diego Luna out for the remainder of the 2026 season after having his meniscus repaired on Friday, and 2026 FIFA World Cup standouts JuanMa Sanabria (Uruguay) and recently-acquired DF Luc de Fougerolles (Canada) away on international duty, Head Coach Pablo Mastroeni looks at his roster of young talent to step up and snap the Club’s winless streak. Despite a lack of scoring firepower over recent fixtures, RSL has proven it has the attacking quality capable of finding the back of the net. Spanish FW Sergi Solans has showcased on countless occasions throughout his rookie MLS campaign. With nine goals and three assists in MLS thus far, the 23-year-old sits atop RSL’s 2026 Golden Boot leaderboard. If the Spaniard can combine his speed, creativity and ability to threaten both with the ball at his feet and his quality in the air on Wednesday, he could end his personal scoring drought and help secure a much-needed RSL win. Running alongside Solans is a trio of creative players who are proven difference-makers on the pitch. RSL Academy product Aiden Hezarkhani, Franco-Guinean designated player Morgan Guilavogui and Georgian international MF Saba Lobjanidze have each netted two goals in MLS play for RSL this season. At just 19 years old, Hezarkhani has established himself as a key contributor, bringing grit and energy to the pitch. RSL’s French-born DP Guilavogui has continuously showcased his high soccer IQ, finding his teammates time and again to earn an impressive seven assists in 2026. With Lobjanidze rounding out the trio with an additional three assists since joining the Club in July, the three players have proven their ability to impact matches with creativity, energy and playmaking abilities, all of which are key to RSL’s chances for victory and snapping its 12-game winless streak on Wednesday. While a midweek win for the Claret-and-Cobalt would snap the Club’s winless streak, a result would also come as a boost for the Utah side which holds a less than favorable road record of 1-8-3 (W-L-T) this season. As RSL looks to earn its second victory away from home in 2026 and its first since March 7 at Atlanta, it is important to look at its head-to-head history with Western Conference opponent Seattle Sounders FC, as well as the key roster pieces for the home side. Since the first meeting between the two sides in 2009, RSL holds a slight edge over Seattle, with an overall record of 20-17-9 (W-L-T), earning three more all-time wins over its opponent across all competitions. The home side has won five of the last six meetings between the teams, with RSL earning a 1-1 draw in Seattle back in 2024. Earlier this season, the Sounders traveled to the Riot for RSL’s home opener on February 28, suffering a 2-1 loss. RSL opened up the scoring with 19-year-old Hezarkhani, who netted his first-ever MLS score in the 23rd minute. Then, Australian FW Ari Piol ultimately scored the game-winner for his lone goal of 2026, unfortunately ending his season in the 82nd minute after suffering a torn achilles. Much like RSL, the Sounders have found itself on an unfavorable run of form in recent months. After defeating the San Jose Earthquakes 3-2 on May 13, Seattle has gone winless in 13 straight matches, earning a record of 0-8-5 (W-L-T) over the five-month span. And although the Claret-and-Cobalt were able to secure a result in the early-season meeting between the two, the rescheduled road matchup will not be an automatic victory. With both sides in dire need of a result, Seattle will look to its weapons to make the game difficult from the opening whistle. One of Seattle's key attacking stars will be absent Wednesday due to the ongoing double FIFA International window. Dynamic MLS veteran Dejan Joveljić, who has earned a spot on the Serbian National Team roster, will miss the midweek matchup. Although the forward recently joined Seattle in August, he has immediately made an impact in the attack, netting three goals in just four matches with his new club. With International duty calling, 27-year-old Paul Rothrock and veteran MF Cristian Roldan remain. Rothrock is the home side's leading scorer in its campaign thus far, having netted five goals and one assist to sit atop the Sounders’ 2026 Golden Boot leaderboard. Roldan sits just behind his teammate with four goals and three assists. Although Seattle will be missing a key piece of its offense in Joveljić, keeping the goal-scoring duo of Rothrock and Roldan quiet will be a crucial task for the defense in order to earn a result. The midweek matchup at Lumen Field is set to kickoff at 7:30 p.m. MT and will be streaming on Apple TV. The Claret-and-Cobalt will then return to America First Field for its second home match of this crowded week this Saturday, September 26, welcoming the New England Revolution to the Wasatch Front. title: Examining the legal complaint in CNN et al v. Trump - Free Speech Center
content: Home » Perspective » Examining the legal complaint in CNN et al v. Trump The lawsuit filed by CNN, MS NOW and Politico against the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump is photographed Monday, Sept. 21, 2026. (AP Photo/Jon Elswick) On Sept. 18, 2026, President Donald J. Trump announced that he was banning reporters from CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO from access they had long enjoyed at the White House. He said he was doing so because of their negative reporting, which he identified as “Fake News.” The next day, Betsy Klein of CNN, Akayla Gardner of MS NOW and Cheyenne Haslett of POLITICO were denied access to the White House, and their hard passes to the premises were revoked. On Monday, Sept. 21, 2026, the organizations filed a complaint for declaratory and injunctive relief in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. Referring to the ban as a “direct assault on the First Amendment” and a “blatant violation of our most fundamental principles,” their complaint argued that they were being targeted on the basis of the “content of their coverage” of the president and his administration in a manner that constituted viewpoint discrimination. The networks said that their ban had been done without proper notice or due process in that they were not given “advance notice based on clear standards and an opportunity to be heard.” On a more technical matter they argued that the White House constituted “a nonpublic forum,” to which, once admitted, organizations could not be excluded on the basis of their viewpoints or on grounds that were unreasonable. In this case they argued that debarring members that the president disliked was “far too vague and arbitrary a standard to qualify as reasonable under the First Amendment and undermines the very purpose of press access to the White House, which is to facilitate fact-based reporting for the benefit of the pubic.” The complaint said that the president’s actions had an adverse effect not only on their businesses but also on the public. They also suggested that the actions would have a chilling effect upon coverage by other news organizations. The complaint indicated that all three networks had long had access to the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room, press spaces in the West Wing, and access to the North Lawn of the White House and had been part of the pool of reporters who accompanied the president and shared reporting, video, and photographs with other news outlets. The complaint noted that in November 2018, a federal court had ordered that the press credentials of Jim Acosta of CNN News should be restored after Trump had attempted to exclude him after an exchange with him that Trump had disliked. The complaint further observed that, in making his announcement, Trump has actually referred to his ban as “the ban on the free press.” He had said that he wasn’t responding to any particular story but to “cumulative stories over the last two years” that constituted “negative” and what he considered to be “dishonest” news. The complaint pointed out that this standard failed to provide fair notice and was effectively void for vagueness. The complaint said that the reporters involved had both “liberty and property interests” in their press passes and access to the White House. They further alleged that their reporters had been subject to unconstitutional retaliation. The decision by the D.C. Circuit Court in Aref v. Lynch, 833 F.3d 242 (2016) had indicated that plaintiffs could establish such retaliation by showing that they were “engaged in conduct protected under the First Amendment,” that they had suffered from retaliation “sufficient to deter a person of ordinary firmness in plaintiff’s position from speaking again,” and that there was a causal link between their exercise of First Amendment rights and the retaliation. The complaint said that the news organizations had met this burden. In elaborating on the doctrine of a “nonpublic forum,” the complaint cited case law to indicate that “any restrictions on access to these press areas be both viewpoint neutral and reasonable in light of the purpose served by the forum,” and that the government had not met either standard. In addition to asking that the president’s action be enjoined and declared unlawful, the complaint asked for reasonable costs and attorneys’ fees. In a show of solidarity, major television networks announced that they will halt their coverage of White House events in the interim. The networks’ complaint appears on solid First Amendment grounds. Judicial rulings permit individuals to sue news organizations for disseminating libelous reports, but they require plaintiffs in cases involving public figures to prove that such reports were made with knowledge that they were false or with reckless disregard for their truth or falsity. U.S. courts have not awarded damages for expressions of opinion, which are clearly protected by the First Amendment, and a characterization of reporting as “fake news” is far too vague a charge to be likely to justify actions against media outlets. Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee who previously ruled in favor of Jim Acosta when the White House had suspended his credentials, has been randomly assigned to the case. John R. Vile is a political science professor and dean of the Honors College at Middle Tennessee State University. title: CCIA Joins Supreme Court Amicus Brief in Apple v. Epic - CCIA
content: Computer & Communication Industry Association Computer & Communication Industry Association Washington – The Computer & Communications Industry Association has filed an amicus brief in support of Apple Inc. in Apple v. Epic. The Supreme Court recently agreed to hear the case. The issue involves whether the district court correctly found Apple in contempt for violating the so-called “spirit” of a court order even where the conduct at issue did not violate any explicit prohibition in the order. In the brief, CCIA, SIIA, and NetChoice pointed out that this “spirit” of the injunction test runs counter to the law of other Circuits – and federal law generally – and also makes it difficult to assess when a company has violated an injunction, because it is unclear what the “spirit” of an order would actually require. The amici tell the Justices that applying a text-based standard for injunctive relief is of interest to tech associations representing a range of companies that use such injunctions when seeking to challenge unconstitutional and otherwise unlawful regulations. “This is a dispute about certainty. Court orders should not leave the public guessing about a judge’s intentions. If they do, it is not a party’s responsibility to divine the court’s intent. This is particularly important for injunctions affecting protected speech and editorial curation, which is protected by the First Amendment.” CCIA is an international, not-for-profit trade association representing a broad cross section of communications and technology firms.
