title: Baby girls’ greater interest in faces offers clue to nature v nurture debate - The Guardian
content: Study finds overall differences between groups of newborns by sex that are likely to be determined by biology The question dates back to the first man and woman: how does the world shape the behaviour of the sexes, and what differences, if any, are present at birth? Untangling the contributions of nature versus nurture has proved challenging for scientists, and controversial at times, but a new study of babies sheds light on at least one aspect of the puzzle. When newborns were played side-by-side videos of a face and a toy, girls spent proportionally more time, on average, watching the face than boys did, suggesting that differences in attention may exist when we are born. Because the babies were only a day or so old it is unlikely the effect was driven by culture or social experience. That leaves biological factors such as genetics and exposure to different levels of testosterone in the womb as the leading suspects. “This is a very active and heated debate in the field of sex differences: what are the causes behind sex differences and how early in life are they present?” said Yumnah Khan, a PhD student at the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge. “What our research shows is that at least some differences are present at a small scale very early on in life.” For the study, babies aged from eight hours to three days old watched a laptop while settled on their parent or carer’s lap. The screen showed side-by-side videos with a young woman’s face on one side and a Newton’s cradle toy on the other. An eye tracker monitored where the babies looked as the video played. Both sexes showed more interest in the video of the woman’s face than the clip of the Newton’s cradle swinging back and forth. But the girls favoured the face over the toy more than the boys did. Details are published in the journal Biology of Sex Differences. The findings, based on tests with 130 babies at the Rosie hospital in Cambridge, reveal average differences between groups of boys and girls; they don’t apply to all girls and all boys. There was still plenty of variation and overlap between each sex, the researchers said. Small differences at birth are unlikely to define how children learn and develop, but they may play a role in some long-observed trends. On average, girls learn to talk earlier than boys, for example, and develop certain social skills at a younger age, too. “If they’re showing heightened social interest from birth onwards, that might facilitate the development of these skills,” said Khan, though this is only a hypothesis. Support for the idea could come from further studies that follow the babies until they are toddlers. Another question the Cambridge team is exploring is whether subtle differences between the sexes at birth have any bearing on people’s vulnerability to neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions. For example, autism and ADHD are more commonly diagnosed in males, while anxiety and depression are more common in females. “That’s the root issue that we’re really trying to understand here when we’re asking are there any differences present in males and females early in life and what causes these differences,” Khan said. Previous work has found similar on-average sex differences in brain structure at birth. These are thought to be driven by hormones in the womb, with male foetuses exposed to more than twice the level of testosterone as females in the first and second trimesters.

title: CR-V Is Destroying RAV4 In America, And Honda Is About To Turn Up The Heat - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update We added a section with details surrounding Nissan's upcoming Rogue Hybrid, which will be a fierce competitor to the current RAV4 and upcoming CR-V Hybrid. Toyota's new, all-hybrid RAV4 line should've been dominating the sales charts this year. It packed fresh styling, more power, and more efficiency in what was already America's favorite vehicle that wasn't an F-Series. Instead, production woes sent sales plummeting early in the year. That's left an opening for its fiercest rival, the Honda CR-V to overtake it. In fact, the Honda is so far ahead, it's unlikely that Toyota can catch up this year. It seems Honda is wanting to hold onto that lead, since it may be launching a new generation of CR-V even earlier than expected. We've known for some time now that Honda has been working up a revised platform and powertrain for its small to midsize hybrids, which include the Civic, CR-V, and Accord. Honda shared details and even demonstrated a test car late last year. At that time, we were expecting to see either a new hybrid Civic or CR-V appear toward the end of 2026. It now seems certain that the CR-V is probably what we'll see, since Japanese news outlet Nikkei reports that production of the new CR-V hybrid will start in Canada in February, followed by its plants in Indiana and Ohio in March. That probably means vehicles arriving at dealers before summer. This new CR-V hybrid will likely be substantially different from the current model, which is a bit of a surprise considering the current one has only been around since the 2023 model year. The big differences will come from the new chassis, which will be lighter and up to 10% cheaper to produce, as well as the updated powertrain. While it will still use a naturally-aspirated 2.0-liter four-cylinder, it will have some improvements to efficiency from direct fuel injection and new electric motors. Honda is also adding the simulated shifting from the Prelude, some interesting power control tricks to aid handling, and, apparently, a surprisingly sporty exhaust note. Ultimately, the Toyota RAV4 may return to glory, especially once the company finally gets production back up to full pace. However, if the new CR-V hybrid delivers on efficiency and cost improvements on top of its great driving dynamics, Toyota should be worried about losing sales. Even worse, though, is that a new Honda won't be the only thing for the RAV4 to face down. Nissan is about to launch its first hybrid Rogue in years. It's on a completely new platform that will eventually be joined by a combustion-only version in the near future, and our experience with a prototype shows that it has serious potential in the segment. Hyundai has also revealed a completely new Tucson for next year with stand-out styling and it's notably bigger. Depending on how these new models perform, the RAV4, which is a heavily refreshed version of its predecessor, could suddenly be at a disadvantage, right as production starts picking up. Some of the most popular cars in the country are the Toyota RAV4 and the Honda CR-V. With the RAV4 already existing as an all-hybrid lineup, and the CR-V's hybrid trim debuting soon, Nissan needs to make a move while it still can. The brand has made its intentions clear: there will be a hybrid Nissan in the most competitive segment in the industry, and it's about to hit your local dealership. We had a chance to drive the 2027 Rogue Hybrid prototype recently — though our time was limited, we got a good feel for its design, space, tech, and powertrain. Firstly, it's surprisingly luxurious when options are installed. Buyers will have the choice to equip their hybrid Rogue with a panoramic sunroof, heated steering wheel, surround view cameras, rear seat heating, front seat ventilation, and much more. The real news surrounds the model's propulsion, though. Under the hood is a 2.5-liter turbocharged inline-3 hybrid system that makes 225 horsepower combined with all-wheel drive. It gets an estimated 40/36/38 mpg city/highway/combined, and it'll tow up to 1,500 pounds. Keep an eye out for our comprehensive full drive review of the production model soon. "Jumping into the Rogue, it sounds and feels like an electric luxury car in comparison. The electric part comes from the fact that it's propelled by electric motors with single-speed transmissions, so there's no shifting, and you get instant torque. It's also possible to have one-pedal driving with regenerative braking." Aside from Toyota having some real reasons to worry about the RAV4's position in the compact SUV segment, Honda moving up CR-V production, and especially the hybrid, says something else. It shows how important hybrids are becoming in the market. Even Nissan has prioritized getting the hybrid version of its new Rogue to market before the combustion one. It's also quite possible that demand for hybrids could grow even more now that gas prices are spiking. In fact, Toyota probably isn't the only company that should be concerned about its position in the car market, but so should American automakers that are lacking small hybrid SUVs. Something with a battery to get me around town and a ICE engine to take over on a long trip. OR, one electric and one gas vehicle in the family would be good also. title: The Trojan Horse Rides Again: On the Swedish Supreme Court’s MFN Ruling in Okuashvili v. Georgia - Wolters Kluwer
content: The Trojan Horse Rides Again: On the Swedish Supreme Court’s MFN Ruling in Okuashvili v. Georgia On 26 June 2026, Sweden’s Supreme Court (“Court”) handed down judgment in Zaza Okuashvili v. Georgia, reversing the Svea Court of Appeal’s judgment and holding that an SCC tribunal could take jurisdiction over a claim against Georgia by combining the most-favored-nation (“MFN”) clause of one treaty with the dispute settlement clause of an entirely different one. The MFN clause’s capacity to reach into dispute settlement has often been described as a Trojan Horse, since contracting parties introduce the clause themselves. The Court has given the horse free rein by allowing an investor to switch arbitral forums via an MFN clause. This post makes two arguments: first, that the Court widened the MFN clause’s scope beyond the limits recognized by previous tribunals; second, that it failed to give due weight to the contextual requirement of State consent, overlooking considerations mandated by Articles 31 and 32 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (“VCLT”). The facts of the case and the Court’s reasoning are set out in a previous Blog post in full (see here), this piece confines itself to two specific respects in which that reasoning falls short. Okuashvili holds both Georgian and British nationality (¶4). Due to Article 25(2)(a) of the ICSID Convention, Okuashvili was barred from arbitrating against his own State “regardless of what other citizenship he or she holds,” and this dual nationality excluded him from Article 8 of the UK-Georgia BIT that only offers ICSID arbitration (¶1, ¶5). The BIT’s MFN clause, Article 3, explicitly extends to Article 1 to 11 (¶2). Georgia’s separate treaty with the Belgo-Luxembourg Economic Union (“BLEU”) lets investors choose among ICSID, the ICC, or the SCC (¶3). Okuashvili used the MFN clause to reach into the BLEU treaty’s more permissive forum and commenced SCC arbitration against Georgia (¶6). The tribunal accepted jurisdiction; however, the Svea Court of Appeal set aside the award (¶7). The Court has now reinstated the tribunal’s approach (¶¶60-62). The intervening procedural history is set out in the previous Blog post referenced above. Two findings of the Court are of importance. The Court held that ICSID and SCC arbitration are “of the same kind” under the ejusdem generis principle, since both are “established arbitration dispute resolution mechanisms” (¶46). It acknowledged that Article 8 reflects the “preferred” ICSID-exclusive version of the UK’s 1991 model investment treaty, deliberately chosen over a version offering investors a choice of fora – yet held that this choice “cannot be given any decisive importance” (¶47). Whether an MFN clause can reach a treaty’s dispute-settlement machinery has been debated for decades. The question was already argued in the 1950s, in the Ambatielos arbitration between Greece and the United Kingdom, where the ICJ confirmed the relevance of the ejusdem generis rule but dismissed the claim on its merits for failing to show any “privileges, favours or immunities… more extensive than those resulting from the basic treaty.” It was Maffezini v. Spain that first used MFN as a weapon to create jurisdiction. The tribunal let an investor skip an eighteen-month local-litigation requirement under the Argentina-Spain BIT by importing a more permissive dispute-settlement clause from Spain’s treaty with Chile, reasoning that dispute settlement is “inextricably related” to investment protection and therefore falls within the clause’s reach (¶¶54-56). Siemens v. Argentina and Gas Natural v. Argentina followed suit, apparently settling the question in the investor’s favour. However, other tribunals placed limitations on this rule. Plama v. Bulgaria and Salini v. Jordan held that an MFN clause cannot import dispute-settlement provisions “unless [it] leaves no doubt that the contracting parties intended to incorporate them” (Plama, ¶223). Wintershall v. Argentina’s stricter interpretation stated that an MFN clause cannot extend to procedural provisions without clear and unambiguous language. By 2015 the split had become pronounced enough that the International Law Commission’s Study Group devoted its entire final report to the MFN clause, concluding that tribunals would keep deciding the question case by case – not exactly the clear boundary needed. (¶216). Two features of Maffezini’s own reasoning are directly relevant here and were overlooked by the Court entirely. The Maffezini tribunal, while expanding the MFN clause to dispute resolution, warned of the consequences and signaled that the clause’s scope should be narrowly construed. It held that the beneficiary of the clause should not be able to override fundamental conditions for acceptance of the agreement, especially if the beneficiary is the private investor (¶62). The tribunal listed the most prominent situations where the clause should not apply, including where “the agreement provides for a particular arbitration forum, such as ICSID, this option cannot be changed by invoking the clause, in order to refer the dispute to a different system of arbitration” (¶63). Okuashvili does swap ICSID for SCC arbitration, precisely what the Maffezini tribunal anticipated and excluded. Plama and Salini confronted investors making this exact move and rejected it. In Plama, the tribunal refused to let a Bulgaria-Cyprus dispute travel from ad hoc arbitration into ICSID arbitration through the MFN clause, applying the “no doubt” standard quoted above (¶223). Salini reached the same conclusion on comparable facts (¶¶102–19). One case might support the Supreme Court’s conclusion: Garanti Koza v. Turkmenistan where the tribunal substituted an exclusive ICSID arbitration clause with another BIT’s dispute resolution clause that gave investors the option between ICSID and UNCITRAL. But that case drew heavy criticism for manufacturing consent the underlying treaty never gave. None of this appears in the Swedish judgment. Instead, the Court works around the exceptions by finding that ICSID and SCC arbitration are “of the same kind” for ejusdem generis purposes, since both are established institutional forms of arbitration (¶46). This observation, while true, answers the wrong question. The forum-substitution exception has nothing to do with how institutions resemble each other; it has to do with whether a particular forum was the price of a State’s consent. Two arbitral institutions can be equally similar, and it will still be true that a State agreed to be sued in one of them and not the other. The extension of an MFN clause may be defensible where it removes an objectively burdensome procedural obligation that places an investor in a less favorable position than investors protected under comparable third-party treaties. The same justification, however, does not extend to investors seeking merely to substitute one arbitral forum for another based on their own interests. The second problem lies in how the Court read the treaty’s drafting history. The Court acknowledged that the UK offered two dispute-settlement templates in its 1991 model investment treaty: an ICSID exclusive “preferred” version, and a “alternative” version letting investors choose among ICSID, the ICC, and ad hoc arbitration (¶47). Georgia and the UK chose the exclusive one. A significant number of UK BITs concluded before 1991 used a single forum by default and the rationale behind introducing a broader template was to let treaty partners decide. Choosing between two available options is a form of expression, and arguably a more reliable one than the text of either option read in isolation, since it shows what the parties considered and rejected as well as what they accepted. The Court rightfully identified that this question should be answered under Articles 31 and 32 of the VCLT. Article 31(1) of the VCLT treats this kind of surrounding practice as part of a treaty’s context. Article 32’s reference to the circumstances of a treaty’s conclusion points the same way. The Court weighs it for exactly one sentence, concluding that the UK’s alternative version “cannot be given any decisive importance in the interpretation,” without elaborating on why this is so. The irony is that the Court had already committed itself to the opposite principle elsewhere in the same judgment invoking  effet utile - the idea that a treaty should be interpreted to avoid redundancy - to justify reading the MFN clause broadly (¶16). But effet utile cuts both ways. If the ICSID-exclusive template can be undone by a later MFN clause, then the “preferred” and “alternative” versions of the UK Model BIT lose their difference: whichever one a State signs, an investor can reach the other anyway. That is not giving effect to the treaty’s drafting choices. This does not mean that MFN clauses should be shut out of dispute settlement. The holdings of previous tribunals, on procedural preconditions, remain sound. The objection here is narrower, and for that reason harder to wave away: on the specific question of substituting one arbitral forum for another, the Court has misapplied the one boundary that was set for that exact maneuver and treated a State’s considered choice between two negotiating templates as though it carried no interpretive weight whatsoever. The case now goes back to the Svea Court of Appeal on a narrow remand (¶61). Whatever that court does with it, other tribunals reading this judgment for guidance on the MFN question would do well to treat it as an outlier rather than a template. ©2025 Wolters Kluwer N.V. and/or its subsidiaries. title: Archie Weatherspoon V Commits as Cal Poly Men's Basketball's Top Recruit Ever - Mustang News
content:
Cal Poly Men’s Basketball has officially landed its highest-rated recruit in program history in combo guard Archie Weatherspoon V. Weatherspoon V, who attends Rangeview High School in Aurora, Colo., announced on Sunday that he plans to join the Mustangs next season. Weatherspoon V is a three-star recruit according to 247Sports and is ranked the 247th player in the country and the third-highest in the state of Colorado. The 6-foot-3 guard held offers from programs such as Cal, Creighton, UNLV and High Point but ultimately opted to join Head Coach Mike DeGeorge and the Mustangs. With a 247Sports composite rating of .8950, Weatherspoon V surpasses Brantly Stevenson (2020) as the outlet’s highest-ranked Cal Poly recruit in history. DeGeorge’s previous coaching stint at Colorado Mesa gave him familiarity with Weatherspoon V’s home state, a potential advantage while recruiting against higher-profile programs. Weatherspoon V profiles as a potential lead guard while remaining a high-level scoring threat, using his 6-foot-8 wingspan to slice through defenses and get to the basket. Weatherspoon V has been highly efficient at the high school level and possesses a clean, repeatable shooting form. Weatherspoon V averaged 19.2 points, 4.0 rebounds, 3.7 assists and 1.6 steals per game across 26 games in his junior season. He is the first verbal commitment that the Mustangs have gotten in this recruiting cycle. Oliver Marburg is the sports copy editor for Mustang News. title: CR-V Laps The RAV4, And Honda Isn't Coasting - thetruthaboutcars.com
content: Toyota's all-new, all-hybrid RAV4 was supposed to spend 2026 doing what the RAV4 always does: sit near the top of the sales charts as the best-selling thing in America that isn't an F-Series. Fresh styling, more power, better efficiency. Instead, production problems knocked sales down early in the year, and the Honda CR-V walked right through the open door. Honda's lead is now large enough that Toyota probably can't reel it back before the calendar runs out. Rather than sit on that advantage, Honda appears to be pressing it. According to Japanese outlet Nikkei, production of a new-generation CR-V hybrid starts in Canada in February, with the Indiana and Ohio plants following in March. That points to cars reaching dealers before summer, sooner than the previously expected late-2026 window. That's a quick turnaround for a model that's only been on sale since the 2023 model year. The changes run deep. Honda's compact and midsize hybrid family — Civic, CR-V, and Accord — has been in line for a reworked architecture and drivetrain, previewed by a running prototype late last year. The new chassis is lighter and reportedly up to 10 percent cheaper to build. The powertrain keeps a naturally aspirated 2.0-liter four but adds direct injection and new electric motors for efficiency. Honda is also porting over the Prelude's simulated shifting, some power-control tricks meant to aid handling, and reportedly a sportier exhaust note. The RAV4 may well recover once Toyota gets production back to full pace. But a cheaper, more efficient CR-V isn't the only thing waiting for it. Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window. Nissan is launching its first hybrid Rogue in years, on an entirely new platform that will later spawn a combustion version. Hyundai has revealed a new Tucson for next year, bigger and with more distinctive styling. Today's RAV4 amounts to a substantial update of the outgoing car rather than a clean-sheet design. Notably, both Honda and Nissan are prioritizing the hybrid variants. With gas prices spiking, that timing looks less like a coincidence and more like where the segment is heading.
